transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-03-10 09:32 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Mendez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Erin Lowe (Redwood CSM); Laura Chen (Nimbus CTO), Marco Diaz (ML Eng), Priya Singh (Infra Eng), Ben Torres (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — prefix caching strategy, hit rates, keys, multi-tenant safety, and how this interacts with batching/quantization and your on-prem plans. Samir will lead the technical run-through.
[00:22] Laura: Sounds good. We're most worried about correctness and data safety, also we want to save token cost on high-frequency prefixes.
[00:35] Samir: Great. I'll start with a baseline — what we mean by prefix caching: we cache the KV cache (the key-value states for transformer attention) for repeated prompt prefixes so downstream token generation can reuse the cached state instead of recomputing. In practice, that means if you have lots of identical or similar instruction prefixes we can get very high per-token savings.
[01:10] Marco: Quick question, do you cache across tenants or per-tenant? We run multi-tenant workloads and some prompts include org-specific tokens.
[01:28] Samir: We recommend tenant-scoped keys by default. So cache keys encode tenant id + prefix fingerprint. That prevents cross-tenant contamination and also helps eviction policies be tenant-aware.
[01:45] Priya: How do you handle PII? Some of our prefixes include user names in the instructions.
[01:55] Jordan: Good callout — we treat sensitive data as a config option: either you opt-in to cache such prefixes, or we can provide a scrub pipeline to hash or redact before caching. Also, for Private deployments we can tie storage encryption to your KMS.
[02:20] Samir: On key design — the typical key we use is something like: sha256(tenant_id || model_variant || prefix_fingerprint || quantization_profile). The quantization_profile part is important when you have different runtimes (fp16 vs int8) because the binary representation and kernel selection can differ.
[02:55] Marco: Wait, quantization changes the shape of the KV cache? I thought quantization only changed weights.
[03:05] Samir: Right, good nuance. Quantization doesn't change logical sequence lengths or dimensions, but it can influence which kernels and memory layout the runtime uses. If you have a cached blob produced by an int8 runtime, it may not be compatible with an fp16 runtime path. So we include the runtime/profile in the key to enforce compatibility.
[03:40] Laura: How big are these cached blobs typically? Memory impact is a concern for our Dedicated pools.
[03:50] Samir: Depends on model and sequence length. For example, a 7B model with 2048 context and 1k prefix can be tens to hundreds of MB per prefix if you store full KV for many layers. But with selective layer hashing and compression, plus TTLs, we often see effective per-prefix sizes in the low tens of MB for average prefixes.
[04:25] Ben: Do you do partial-prefix caching? Like store only the most expensive initial layers?
[04:30] Samir: Yes — partial or layered caching is an optimization. You can cache early layers which give most of the compute benefit; it's a tradeoff between hit-rate and storage. We also support prefix summarization where we canonicalize similar prefixes into a single fingerprint to boost hit-rate.
[04:55] Marco: About canonicalization, are there false positives where different prompts collapse and produce incorrect output?
[05:05] Samir: We avoid semantic hash collisions by combining lexical fingerprints with structural cues — e.g., placeholders for user names. But yes, there is always a risk; we recommend a conservative summarization strategy for safety-critical contexts.
[05:30] [06:00] Speaker 1 (background): mhm
[06:10] Priya: For multi-tenant safety, you mentioned salted hashes. Can you elaborate?
[06:20] Samir: Sure. Salted hashing means the fingerprint uses a tenant-specific salt so two tenants with the same prompt won't share a key. This is the primary protection against leakage via cache hits. On top of that, we recommend RBAC and per-tenant encryption, and audit logs to trace cache read/write operations — especially important for SOC2/ISO audits.
[06:50] Jordan: Ops note — in Redwood Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key wrapping of cached blobs and maintain audit trails in your VPC.
[07:10] Laura: What about eviction? If we have hot prefixes from a single tenant, they could monopolize the cache.
[07:22] Samir: We support tenant-weighted eviction and quotas. Policies include LRU per-tenant, global LRU with per-tenant reservations, and explicit pinning for critical prefixes. You can configure reservoir sizes per tenant in Dedicated.
[07:50] Marco: Any guidance on TTLs? We have prompts that change weekly.
[07:58] Samir: TTLs often match content churn — short-lived prompts get 1-6 hours, templates that are stable can be multi-day. For model rollouts we also recommend cache invalidation on model_variant change — that's why model_variant is in the key.
[08:28] Ben: How are hit-rates measured? We want to know expected ROI.
[08:34] Samir: We provide a hit-rate dashboard; metrics include global hit-rate, tenant-level hit-rate, prefix frequency distribution, and token-saved-per-minute. You can also run synthetic replay workloads to estimate gains. Typical hit-rates for templated assistant prompts are 30-60% on the prefix level, but depends highly on how canonicalized your prefixes are.
[09:05] Marco: Is there a cold-start penalty when code first warms the cache?
[09:10] Samir: Yes — first lookups need to compute the KV cache. We support background warming via scheduled batch jobs that precompute popular prefixes. Also, we have on-demand pre-warming APIs.
[09:30] Priya: For on-prem deployments, how is the cache stored? On NVMe, in GPU memory, or remote?
[09:40] Samir: Several options: hot caches in GPU memory for sub-ms reuse, warm caches on local NVMe, and cold caches in encrypted object storage. The policy picks where to store based on latency SLOs and frequency. GPU memory caching gives the best latency but is smallest; NVMe is a good middle ground.
[10:05] Laura: Do you support cross-region replication for caches? Our users are global.
[10:12] Samir: We can replicate hot cache entries to regional nodes, but cross-region replication increases complexity and consistency issues. Often better to route requests to region-local caches with smart routing to avoid cross-region hops.
[10:35] Jordan: Let's talk about security: you mentioned audit logs for cache reads — do you store the plaintext prompt in logs?
[10:45] Erin: We generally store hashed fingerprints in logs and can redact full prompts. For customers who need full logging, we can support encrypted logs with restricted access.
[11:05] Marco: Regarding batching: how does continuous batching interact with prefix cache hits?
[11:12] Samir: When a request hits the prefix cache, it reduces per-token compute, which can reduce batching efficiency because batches are less balanced. Our runtime supports adaptive batching: if many requests are cache-hits and a few are not, we route the non-hits separately to maximize throughput. There's a tradeoff — batching increases throughput but can add latency; cache hits lower compute and can improve latency.
[11:50] Priya: Can caching cause reordering or token interleaving issues with streaming responses?
[11:58] Samir: Streaming is orthogonal — if you have a cached prefix, streaming still sends tokens as they're generated. The runtime maintains KV state per-stream. The only risk is misaligned cache usage across streaming vs non-streaming paths; we mitigate by normalizing key semantics and ensuring streaming requests use the same cache lookup path.
[12:25] Ben: Do we have examples of customers that saw concrete savings?
[12:30] Jordan: We had a conversation with a customer (internal name 'AutoWrite') who saw 42% token cost reduction on templated document generation after canonicalization and prefix caching.
[12:45] Marco: Any performance numbers you can share from Redwood Dedicated? Latency P50/P95 with and without prefix caching?
[12:55] Samir: Rough numbers: without caching, P50 token latency on a 7B model ~7-12ms/token depending on hardware; with a hot GPU-memory prefix hit, we see P50 ~3-5ms/token. P95 depends on batching — with adaptive batching and cache hits you can reduce tail latency significantly, but exact numbers depend on model and infra. We'll share a benchmark spreadsheet.
[13:35] [14:00] Speaker 2 (client): okay thanks
[14:10] Marco: There's also the question of cache poisoning attacks — an adversarial tenant trying to evict or overload caches. How do we mitigate?
[14:22] Samir: Rate limiting and per-tenant quotas are first line. Ensure tenants can't drive eviction by setting strict per-tenant memory reservations and request throttles. Also monitor for abnormal prefix frequency spikes and set alerting.
[14:50] Priya: For encryption, if cached blobs are encrypted with KMS and we rotate keys, does that invalidate cache?
[14:58] Samir: Key rotation strategy matters. We support key wrapping so rotation does not require immediate invalidation — we can re-wrap objects lazily. But if you choose to re-encrypt aggressively you may see temporary cache misses until re-warm. We can coordinate rotations with a scheduled warming window.
[15:28] Laura: Model rollouts worry me — we might change from a curated model to an updated checkpoint. How do you ensure cache validity across rollouts?
[15:40] Samir: Include model_variant & model_checksum in cache keys and invalidate on rollout. For canary/gradual rollouts we recommend maintaining parallel caches for old/new variants and routing requests based on rollout policy. That avoids cross-variant reads.
[16:05] Marco: Can we reuse prefixes between similar model families? Like from a 7B to an 8B family?
[16:12] Samir: Not safely — different architectures or layer counts mean KV semantics differ. You would need a compatibility layer which we don't recommend. Better to recompute for different families.
[16:35] Ben: How do you measure correctness regression introduced by caching and canonicalization?
[16:42] Samir: We tie caching changes into our eval pipeline: we run a curated eval set of prompts comparing outputs with and without caching/canonicalization. If deviation exceeds a threshold we flag it. We also use human-in-the-loop for sensitive domains.
[17:00] Marco: Any tooling for inspecting a cache entry? For debugging?
[17:06] Samir: Yes — in the Redwood Console you can inspect cache keys, hit timestamps, tenant id, size, and whether it was compressed or partial. For Private deployments we can expose a read-only diagnostic endpoint under RBAC.
[17:30] Priya: On the operational side, how do backups work for caches? Do you persist them as part of stateful snapshots?
[17:38] Samir: Caches are ephemeral by design; we don't typically backup caches. For warming we persist a set of pinned prefixes and a manifest so a restore can re-warm automatically. If you need long-lived precomputed state, that's more of a model artifact and we handle it as part of release artifacts under version control.
[18:05] Jordan: Quick interjection — for your Dedicated cluster we can allocate a pinned cache reservoir to guarantee hot prefixes are always in GPU memory.
[18:20] Marco: Would that impact other tenants' latency?
[18:25] Samir: It could if not sized properly, but with tenant reservations and quotas you avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[18:40] Laura: Let's talk about metrics we'll need for your benchmark. We want hit-rate by prefix, token-saved, per-tenant storage footprint, P50/P95 latency with and without cache, and CPU/GPU utilization delta.
[18:55] Samir: We'll include those metrics. Samir: Also we'll produce a breakdown by quantization profile so you can see tradeoffs across fp16 vs int8 kernels.
[19:10] Marco: For the benchmark, can you run a replay of our production traces?
[19:15] Samir: Yes — if you can provide a sanitized trace or sampling, we can replay it in our benchmark harness. For Private/on-prem we can ship a runnable harness you run locally and we'll ingest the metrics.
[19:34] Priya: We have strict compliance — anything stored in cache must be encrypted at rest and have an audit trail. Can that be guaranteed for Private?
[19:43] Erin: Yes — Private supports KMS integration, audit logs, and we can configure log retention. We'll share the SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[20:00] [20:30] Jordan: One more nuance on TTLs and consistency: if you update a prompt template, you might want to evict a small set of prefixes. We support targeted eviction APIs by key or by fingerprint prefix, and wildcard evictions for templated families.
[20:55] Marco: Do you have recommendations for fingerprinting libraries? Some of our current hashing yields collisions for long templates.
[21:05] Samir: We recommend a two-phase fingerprint: first normalize (strip whitespace, canonicalize placeholders), then compute a cryptographic hash (sha256) with a tenant salt. For large templates, also include a lightweight structural hash to detect near-similarity. We'll share our canonicalization code snippet.
[21:35] Ben: What about telemetry — how frequently do you sample to avoid overhead?
[21:42] Samir: Typically we emit per-request sample telemetry at 1-5% for detailed traces and aggregate metrics at 100% (counts, hits/misses). Detailed traces for only a small sample keeps overhead low.
[22:05] Priya: Does prefix caching help with embeddings or only generation models?
[22:12] Samir: Prefix caching is generation-oriented (KV caches). For embeddings you can use vector caching (embedding result cache) which behaves differently but same safety considerations apply.
[22:30] Marco: Let's talk about cost model — how do we estimate storage cost vs token savings?
[22:37] Samir: We'll provide a cost model that takes your prefix distribution, average prefix size, expected hit-rate, and infra cost for GPU/NVMe to calculate net savings. Our earlier customers saw net positive savings once hit-rate crossed about 20-25% depending on infra costs.
[22:58] Laura: Any gotchas with conversational contexts where prefixes grow over time?
[23:05] Samir: For chats we frequently use incremental caching: store KV states at earlier turns and only compute deltas for appended turns. That reduces recompute and is more cache-friendly. But you need versioning so if the model checkpoint changes, you rebase.
[23:40] Ben: Are there recommendations for user-facing behaviors? Like indicating stale answers when cache used?
[23:48] Samir: Usually we keep cache transparent; however for high-sensitivity apps, you can annotate outputs with 'cached' metadata in response headers and optionally surface to users.
[24:05] Marco: About caching across A/B tests — we often run experiments. Would cache hits leak between variants?
[24:12] Samir: No if you include experiment ID in the key. That's the recommended pattern.
[24:30] Priya: For the Private deployment, what are the operational knobs we get?
[24:35] Samir: You get full config for TTLs, eviction policies, per-tenant quotas, pinning, KMS integration, and the warming harness. Also dashboarding endpoints for hit-rate and cost.
[24:58] Laura: Ok, can you summarize recommended defaults for us?
[25:05] Samir: Defaults we recommend: tenant-scoped keys with sha256(tenant||model_variant||quant_profile||prefix_fp), per-tenant quotas with a small pinned reservoir, TTLs of 6h for dynamic templates and 72h for stable templates, background pre-warm for top 100 prefixes, and include runtime profile in the key.
[25:35] Jordan: We'll include a one-pager with those defaults.
[25:45] Marco: About canonicalization thresholds — what threshold for merging do you suggest?
[25:52] Samir: Start very conservative: only merge prompts that differ in known placeholders. Move to fuzzy canonicalization after you validate with evals.
[26:10] Ben: Anything we should avoid?
[26:15] Samir: Avoid cross-tenant cache sharing, avoid aggressive canonicalization without eval, and be cautious with long TTLs if content changes frequently. Also be careful with keying that omits model_variant or quantization profile.
[26:40] [27:00] Speaker 3 (client): okay
[27:10] Priya: For the benchmark Samir will run, can we get the config he uses? We want reproducibility.
[27:18] Samir: Absolutely — we'll share the harness config and the sample workload. For your replay we'll need sanitized traces.
[27:35] Marco: Could you talk briefly about implementation complexity — is prefix caching something that requires model changes?
[27:43] Samir: No model changes. It's runtime-level caching of KV states. The tricky bits are runtime memory management and ensuring consistent serialization across quantized kernels.
[28:05] Laura: Any latency implications for first token after a cache hit?
[28:12] Samir: First token is typically generated faster because attention state is already present; we still have to run the final output layer(s), but you avoid the heavy prefix compute. So you generally see improved P50 and P95.
[28:35] Ben: On the topic of cache observability, can you alert when hit-rate drops?
[28:40] Samir: Yes — we support alerts on hit-rate per-tenant and global, and can tie alerts to deployment events like model rollouts.
[29:00] Marco: How about charging — do you meter cache usage separately?
[29:06] Jordan: For Redwood Hosted we include cache benefits within token billing but provide a token-saved metric. For Dedicated/Private we can offer chargebacks with a storage-based metric if you want to bill teams.
[29:30] Priya: Any integration needed with our CI/CD? We want cache invalidation to happen when prompt templates are updated via code.
[29:40] Samir: We have API hooks for programmatic eviction; many customers integrate eviction into their deployment pipelines so a template change triggers targeted invalidation.
[30:02] Laura: Ok team let's open the floor to any remaining questions.
[30:10] Marco: One micro detail — how do you handle varying seq lengths? If some requests have long prefixes and others short, how do you canonicalize?
[30:20] Samir: Use normalized prefix trimming: canonicalize to a fixed context window for fingerprinting (e.g., last N tokens of the prefix) and optionally store multiple fingerprint granularities for different lengths.
[30:40] Ben: For our test, can we start with top-50 prefixes and see incremental gains?
[30:45] Samir: Yes that's a common approach — optimize for top percentile first.
[30:55] [31:20] Jordan: We'll wrap up with next steps: Jordan will send docs; Samir will run benchmark; Priya to send traces; schedule follow-up next week.
[31:40] Laura: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[31:48] Marco: Thanks, bye.
[31:52] Priya: Bye
[31:55] Erin: Thanks, we'll follow up.
[57:45] (call ended)
